persons.name: Bora Özkent
persons.digest:
Bora Özkent's bulletin from yesterday explains why the Nasdaq is ignoring interest rates: in his view it is not the market but the right companies that are rising, and S&P 500 corporate profits are at record levels. Nvidia hit a record high, SpaceX rose 7.6% in a single day and he is invested "up to his neck" in stocks; but he lists the risks that could end the party as a failed Anthropic IPO, a pullback in stocks and a credit squeeze. On rates, he says hedge funds are running record short positions in 10-year futures, which is why he closed his losing TLT position for tax reasons, though he plans to buy it back. He recommends staying away from Europe: the euro is at a 17-month low against the dollar.

On stocks, he keeps his memory shortage thesis on Micron and thinks Intel's core problems are not over. He adds that a pullback may come toward the elections but that he is holding his portfolio largely in stocks.

items.title: Why Is the Nasdaq Ignoring Interest Rates?
items.summary: Bora Özkent explains the Nasdaq hitting records despite high rates, expensive oil and geopolitical risk through corporate profits: S&P 500 pre-tax profit of $4.7 trillion, annual free cash flow of $4.6 trillion, driven by AI companies. Yesterday the S&P 500 rose 0.67% and the Nasdaq 1.05%; in his view it is the right stocks rising, not the market, while value stocks lag. The risks that could end the party are a failed Anthropic IPO, a pullback in equities, and OpenAI and Anthropic's dependence on new credit and investors. He says hedge funds hold a record 2.04 million contracts of shorts in 10-year futures (historical average about 1 million); he closed his losing TLT position yesterday for tax reasons but plans to buy it again. The euro is at a 17-month low against the dollar; he says to stay away from Europe and that Europe-China tension could fuel inflation. Nvidia is at an all-time high with about $350 billion left to $6 trillion; he does not find it expensive given Foxconn's 47% revenue rise and the forward P/E falling from 25-26 to 19.8. On Micron he relays Barron's view of a 36% rise in memory prices in August and a shortage lasting to 2030; on Intel he says it cannot make GPUs and its core problems persist. SpaceX rose 7.6% yesterday and a report sees a price around $300; he still finds it very expensive and sees sharp-selloff risk if markets turn. He says a pullback may come toward the elections but he himself is invested "up to his neck" in stocks.

persons.name: Heisenberg
persons.digest: Heisenberg makes two valuation critiques today. To those claiming a $2 trillion company could grow 200x to $400 trillion, he points out that the combined value of all stock markets worldwide is $160 trillion. In another reply he explains a stock falling from $1,200 to $760 through the role of margins in valuation, and also asks why margins are not rising at **MU**.

items.title: Valuation pushback on the 200x growth thesis
items.summary: Heisenberg notes that a $2 trillion company growing 200x would be worth $400 trillion, while all the world's stock markets together are worth $160 trillion.

items.title: The role of margins in valuation
items.summary: Heisenberg writes that he warned when people called the stock "super cheap" at $1,200, that it fell to the gap area at $760 and that buyers of calls with inflated IV saw their premiums melt. He says the direction of margins determines valuation and today's cheap stock can look expensive tomorrow if margins contract.

persons.name: Ahmet Sunelcan
persons.digest:
Ahmet Sunelcan is gradually reducing his AI hardware positions at prices he can get, and moving into smaller weights in story stocks that have fallen 60-90% in a year and technologies with breakout potential. In line with this he trimmed **CRDO** and **SMTC**, added **OKLO** to the portfolio, increased **ASTS** and shared **PENG**'s strong earnings. On an optics stock he says his cost is $151 and that he trims as it rises, and he says he has never found Palo Alto cheap.

On the macro side he sees unprofitability and heavy capex in AI as a major risk and views Europe as an indebted, aging continent with no growth.
